content: Urinary tract infections (UTIs) in children occur when bacteria invade the urinary system, which is normally sterile. In healthy individuals, urine in the bladder and the urethra typically does not contain bacteria or has too few to cause an infection. However, any part of the urinary tract can become infected. UTIs are the second most common infection in children and are caused by bacteria entering the urethral opening, traveling upward to the bladder, and sometimes reaching the kidneys. In severe cases, bacteria may enter the bloodstream from the kidneys, leading to sepsis or infections in other organs. During infancy, boys are more likely to develop UTIs, but after infancy, girls are at a significantly higher risk. Children with UTIs often have structural abnormalities in their urinary system, such as vesicoureteral reflux (VUR), which allows urine to flow backward from the bladder to the kidneys, or conditions that obstruct urine flow. These abnormalities increase susceptibility to infections. Delayed diagnosis and treatment of UTIs in children, especially infants, can lead to progressive renal scarring. The primary goals of UTI management are to relieve symptoms, prevent kidney damage, and reduce recurrence by identifying and addressing structural or functional predisposing factors. Treating underlying voiding dysfunction and constipation is also crucial for successful management. Historically, since the 1970s, clinicians have focused on identifying occult bacteremia in febrile infants without a clear source of infection. With the advent of effective vaccines against Haemophilus influenzae type b and Streptococcus pneumoniae, the urinary tract has become recognized as the most frequent site of serious bacterial infections in febrile infants. Diagnosing UTIs in infants can be challenging due to nonspecific symptoms and the need for invasive methods, such as urethral catheterization or suprapubic aspiration, to obtain reliable urine specimens. Delays in treating pyelonephritis increase the risk of renal damage. UTIs can be classified based on the site of infection (bladder, kidney, or urethra), severity (complicated vs. uncomplicated), and recurrence (first or recurrent). These classifications influence clinical management. In healthy children, the urinary tract is sterile, but the urethra is colonized with bacteria. UTIs occur when pathogens enter the urinary tract and adhere to its lining. Normal voiding usually clears pathogens, but conditions like urinary malformations, urine stasis, or impaired urine flow increase the risk of infection. Congenital obstructive uropathy and detrusor-sphincter dyssynergia are also associated with UTIs. Pathogens can also be introduced via foreign bodies or instruments, such as catheters. UTIs are the third most common nosocomial infection, particularly in intensive care units, and are often associated with urethral catheterization. Escherichia coli accounts for 80–90% of UTIs in children. Symptoms of pyelonephritis include fever, chills, flank pain, and costovertebral angle tenderness. Lower urinary tract symptoms include suprapubic pain, dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, cloudy or malodorous urine, and suprapubic tenderness. A urinalysis and urine culture should be performed when a UTI is suspected. Prompt antibiotic therapy is indicated for symptomatic UTIs based on clinical findings and positive urinalysis, even before culture results are available. UTIs are more common in females and uncircumcised male infants. Toilet training in toddlers can lead to voluntary holding of urine and bladder stasis, promoting UTIs. Over 30% of children with UTIs experience recurrence, with risk factors including VUR and bladder-bowel dysfunction. Older non-continent children, such as those with developmental delays, are also at higher risk. The most common pathogens causing UTIs are enteric bacteria, particularly E. coli. Other gram-negative organisms include Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterobacter, and occasionally Pseudomonas. Proteus mirabilis is common in males and children with kidney stones. Gram-positive pathogens include group B Streptococcus and Enterococcus in neonates and infants, reflecting maternal colonization, and Staphylococcus saprophyticus in adolescent girls. Fungal infections, such as those caused by Candida, are rare and typically occur in immunocompromised children or those with long-term indwelling catheters. Viral infections, such as those caused by adenovirus or BK virus, are more common in immunocompromised patients and can lead to hemorrhagic cystitis. Differentiating UTIs from other diseases is essential, as fever may be the only symptom in children under 24 months. Alternative diagnoses include otitis media, gastroenteritis, and upper respiratory tract infections. Occult bacteremia should also be considered, though it is less likely than a UTI in fully immunized children. In verbal children, urinary calculi, urethritis (including sexually transmitted infections), dysfunctional elimination, and diabetes mellitus should be considered. Neonates and infants are at higher risk for UTIs due to their immature immune systems. Breastfeeding appears to protect against UTIs, as breast milk contains higher levels of IgA. Approximately 8% of girls and 2% of boys experience at least one UTI by age 7. The incidence of UTIs is similar in boys and girls under 2 years of age but becomes more common in girls as they grow older, particularly in sexually active teenagers. Uncircumcised infant boys are at higher risk for UTIs. Structural abnormalities, neurologic deficiencies, or voiding dysfunction resulting in residual urine can contribute to persistent bacteriuria. In developed countries, UTIs are more common in white girls than in girls of other races, with a lower incidence in African-American children. Common complications of UTIs in children include kidney abscesses, reduced kidney function or failure, hydronephrosis (swelling of the kidneys), and sepsis, which can lead to organ failure and death. Prognosis is generally good with immediate treatment, but some children may require long-term treatment, especially if diagnosed with VUR. This condition increases the risk of kidney infections, damage, and failure. Surgery may be necessary in severe cases, though mild or moderate VUR often resolves with time. Kidney damage or failure may still occur in adulthood. Fever is the most common presentation of UTIs in young children. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends ruling out UTIs in children aged 2 months to 2 years with unexplained fever. In younger children, the presence of upper respiratory infections, otitis media, or gastroenteritis does not exclude the possibility of a UTI. Recurrent abdominal pain in this age group may indicate recurrent UTIs and should be promptly evaluated. In older children, fever is also a common symptom, along with vomiting, loose stools, and abdominal pain. Specific symptoms of cystitis or pyelonephritis, such as dysuria, frequency, new-onset incontinence, flank pain, and fever, may also be present. Adolescent girls may have urethritis from sexually transmitted infections, necessitating laboratory evaluation. Urinalysis and urine culture are essential for diagnosing UTIs. In infants and young children who are not toilet-trained, urine samples are obtained via catheterization to avoid contamination. Contaminated samples can lead to inaccurate results. Urine culture identifies the type and quantity of bacteria causing the infection and guides antibiotic treatment. Imaging tests, such as ultrasound, are recommended for children under 2 years with febrile UTIs, those with recurrent infections, or those with high blood pressure, poor growth, or a family history of kidney or bladder problems. A voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) may be performed to assess for VUR. Treatment of acute uncomplicated UTIs typically involves secondor third-generation cephalosporins or amoxicillin-clavulanate. Parenteral antibiotic therapy is recommended for infants under 2 months or children who are toxic-appearing, hemodynamically unstable, immunocompromised, unable to tolerate oral medication, or not responding to oral treatment. Continuous antimicrobial prophylaxis may be considered for children with frequent febrile UTIs, though it does not reduce the risk of recurrence in children with mild to moderate VUR. The duration of treatment depends on the severity of the infection, symptom resolution, and the presence of recurrent infections or urinary tract abnormalities. Surgical intervention is considered only when medical management fails, defined as recurrent infections, pyelonephritis, or poor renal growth. Preventive measures include adequate fluid intake, good bathroom and diapering habits, wearing loose-fitting clothing, and avoiding constipation. Addressing related health problems may also help prevent UTIs.
